rationale: A wins because it stays inside the facts and still finds real tension: "Instacart's ad business hit a $1B run rate while its core delivery growth fell to single digits" is a pitchable contrarian frame with the right proof demands attached. B has sharper raw instincts, but "A cart that watches what you put in it is now the grocery aisle's newest ad surface" asserts the cart-ad connection the update never gives. I can fix a missed angle; I cannot pitch a fact I don't have.
gaps_in_A: "Caper smart carts let shoppers skip the checkout line — and they're spreading to more chains" is the weakest angle because it is still vendor-rollout news until a named retailer provides operating results.
"Over 6,000 brands now advertise on a grocery-delivery app — what that says about retail media" is directionally right but a little generic; the buyer-side protagonist is underdeveloped.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is slightly premature when the set itself admits there may be no live external peg. Find the peg or proof first, then build the list.
gaps_in_B: "A cart that watches what you put in it is now the grocery aisle's newest ad surface" overclaims. The update says carts track items and Instacart sells ads; it does not say carts are ad inventory.

"the cart rollout and the ad-revenue milestone are being disclosed at the same time, which is what makes the connection reportable rather than speculative" is bad logic. Same-day disclosure is not evidence of a business connection.

"a few hundred stores across a 1,500-plus banner network — meaning the vast majority of banners have not deployed them" needs cleaner proof. Store count and banner count are not interchangeable enough for that line to carry itself.
"this beat has already seen fail twice" is unsupported beat lore. If you mean Amazon Go or another failed checkout tech wave, name the evidence or cut the wink.
